The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: The density $\phi$ in [F1] is positive and continuous by [F2]. Fix $a<b$. By [F3], $\phi$ attains a minimum $c$ on $[a,b]$; since $\phi$ is positive at every point, $c>0$. The density formula and additivity over $(-\infty,a]\sqcup(a,b]$ give $\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)=\int_{(a,b]}\phi(x)\,dx\ge c(b-a)>0$, so $\Phi$ is strictly increasing.

Fix $x\in\mathbb R$. By [F3], $\phi$ is bounded by some finite $M$ on the compact interval $[x-1,x+1]$. If $|y-x|<1$, then $|\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)|\le M|y-x|$ by integrating the density over the interval between $x$ and $y$. Letting $y\to x$ proves continuity at $x$, and $x$ was arbitrary.

The sets $(-\infty,n]$ increase to $\mathbb R$, so [F4] and the total mass in [F1] give $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi(n)=1$. The sets $(-\infty,-n]$ decrease to the empty set and have finite measure, so [F5] gives $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi(-n)=0$. Monotonicity from step 1.1 then gives the two stated limits at infinity.

boundaries.reason: The CDF is defined on the full nonempty real line; the statement makes no claim about an empty domain.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 proves the lower-tail limit is zero; step 1.1 proves strict increase across every interval with a<b.
Step 2.1 proves the upper-tail limit is one from the total mass of the normal law.

boundaries.reason: The standard normal law is fixed with variance one; no degenerate normal law is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 obtains both limits as x tends to negative and positive infinity.
The Statement assumes AC through the standard-normal construction; steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 use fixed real points and supplied measure/calculus facts, with no further selection.

boundaries.reason: No equivalence or forward implication is asserted.
No equivalence or reverse implication is asserted.

axiom_uses.reason: AC is required through the standard-normal law used in F1; the density, interval and measure-continuity arguments introduce no stronger choice use.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–2.1 independently checked against the current normal-law definition, exponential smoothness, compact extreme values and both measure-continuity statements. Positive compact minimum gives strict increase for all a<b; local finite bound gives continuity; increasing/decreasing half-lines give both infinite limits, with finite probability for continuity from above. AC inherited only. No reader/refuter finding or defect.

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge0$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and a fixed nonzero vector $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise. Define the projection matrix and contrast direction
$$P_\eta=\frac{\eta\eta^T}{\|\eta\|^2},\qquad c_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\|\eta\|^2}.$$
The matrix $P_\eta$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, put
$$T(y)=\eta^Ty,\qquad Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y.$$
Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

For row $j$ of $A$, written $a_j^T$, define
$$r_j=a_j^Tc_\eta,\qquad d_j(z)=b_j-a_j^Tz.$$
Let $J_-=\{j:r_j<0\}$, $J_+=\{j:r_j>0\}$, and $J_0=\{j:r_j=0\}$. Define
$$L(z)=\begin{cases}\max_{j\in J_-}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_-\ne\varnothing,\\-\infty,&J_-=\varnothing,\end{cases}\qquad U(z)=\begin{cases}\min_{j\in J_+}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_+\ne\varnothing,\\+\infty,&J_+=\varnothing.\end{cases}$$
Define $G(z)$ to hold exactly when $d_j(z)\ge0$ for every $j\in J_0$. The selection event is $S=\{y:Ay\le b\}$. The interval associated with $z$ is $I(z)=\varnothing$ if $G(z)$ fails or $L(z)>U(z)$, and is $[L(z),U(z)]$ otherwise. The next lemma proves that this interval describes precisely the fiber of $S$ along the contrast direction.

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge0$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and a fixed nonzero vector $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise. Define the projection matrix and contrast direction
$$P_\eta=\frac{\eta\eta^T}{\|\eta\|^2},\qquad c_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\|\eta\|^2}.$$
The matrix $P_\eta$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, put
$$T(y)=\eta^Ty,\qquad Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y.$$
Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

For row $j$ of $A$, written $a_j^T$, define
$$r_j=a_j^Tc_\eta,\qquad d_j(z)=b_j-a_j^Tz.$$
Let $J_-=\{j:r_j<0\}$, $J_+=\{j:r_j>0\}$, and $J_0=\{j:r_j=0\}$. Define
$$L(z)=\begin{cases}\max_{j\in J_-}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_-\ne\varnothing,\\-\infty,&J_-=\varnothing,\end{cases}\qquad U(z)=\begin{cases}\min_{j\in J_+}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_+\ne\varnothing,\\+\infty,&J_+=\varnothing.\end{cases}$$
Define $G(z)$ to hold exactly when $d_j(z)\ge0$ for every $j\in J_0$. The selection event is $S=\{y:Ay\le b\}$. The interval associated with $z$ is $I(z)=\varnothing$ if $G(z)$ fails or $L(z)>U(z)$, and is $[L(z),U(z)]$ otherwise. The next lemma proves that this interval describes precisely the fiber of $S$ along the contrast direction.

derivations.claim: Since $P_\eta y=c_\eta(\eta^Ty)=c_\eta T(y)$ and $Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y$, we have $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$.

For each row $j$, the inequality $a_j^Ty\le b_j$ becomes $r_jT(y)\le d_j(Z(y))$. If $r_j>0$, division gives $T(y)\le d_j(Z(y))/r_j$; if $r_j<0$, division reverses the inequality and gives $T(y)\ge d_j(Z(y))/r_j$; if $r_j=0$, the row is feasible exactly when $d_j(Z(y))\ge0$. Intersecting the finitely many row conditions is therefore equivalent to $G(Z(y))$, $T(y)\ge L(Z(y))$, and $T(y)\le U(Z(y))$, with the empty-index conventions in [F2].

Each $d_j$ is affine and hence continuous. The finite maximum defining $L$ and finite minimum defining $U$ are Borel, with the constant infinite values in the empty-index cases; $G$ is a finite intersection of closed half-spaces. Thus the fiber set is Borel. The rowwise equivalence in step 2.1 proves both implications, including zero coefficients and empty or degenerate intervals.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 uses the empty-index conventions for upper or lower row sets, including the case with no truncation rows.
Step 2.1 treats r_j=0 separately and shows feasibility exactly when d_j(Z) is nonnegative.
The Statement permits n=1 with eta nonzero; step 1.1 uses the same projection decomposition in that case.
Step 3.1 explicitly includes L=U and empty intervals in the rowwise equivalence.
The Definition permits infinite endpoints, and step 2.1 preserves the closed inequalities at finite endpoints.
Step 2.1 intersects finitely many row conditions and uses finite maxima/minima only; no choice principle is used.
Step 2.1 derives the zero-row condition and lower/upper interval bounds from Ay<=b.
Step 2.1 shows G and L<=T<=U imply each row inequality, including zero coefficients.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–3.1 checked against the selection definition and orthogonal projection. Row division is reversible for each positive, negative and zero coefficient. Empty m and empty sign sets give the infinite endpoints; inconsistent and singleton intervals are included. Finite extrema of affine functions are Borel and zero-row feasibility is closed, so both directions and measurable fibers hold. No choice use or reader/refuter finding; no defect.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$, and let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $r$, where $0\le r\le n$. Then the random vectors $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent, and
$$
\|PZ\|^2\sim\chi_r^2,\qquad \|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-r}^2.
$$
The two squared norms are independent. The cases $r=0$ and $r=n$ are included, with $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge0$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and a fixed nonzero vector $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise. Define the projection matrix and contrast direction
$$P_\eta=\frac{\eta\eta^T}{\|\eta\|^2},\qquad c_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\|\eta\|^2}.$$
The matrix $P_\eta$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, put
$$T(y)=\eta^Ty,\qquad Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y.$$
Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

For row $j$ of $A$, written $a_j^T$, define
$$r_j=a_j^Tc_\eta,\qquad d_j(z)=b_j-a_j^Tz.$$
Let $J_-=\{j:r_j<0\}$, $J_+=\{j:r_j>0\}$, and $J_0=\{j:r_j=0\}$. Define
$$L(z)=\begin{cases}\max_{j\in J_-}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_-\ne\varnothing,\\-\infty,&J_-=\varnothing,\end{cases}\qquad U(z)=\begin{cases}\min_{j\in J_+}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_+\ne\varnothing,\\+\infty,&J_+=\varnothing.\end{cases}$$
Define $G(z)$ to hold exactly when $d_j(z)\ge0$ for every $j\in J_0$. The selection event is $S=\{y:Ay\le b\}$. The interval associated with $z$ is $I(z)=\varnothing$ if $G(z)$ fails or $L(z)>U(z)$, and is $[L(z),U(z)]$ otherwise. The next lemma proves that this interval describes precisely the fiber of $S$ along the contrast direction.

derivations.claim: Put $P=P_\eta$. Since $\eta\ne0$, $P^T=P$ and $P^2=P$. For every $y$, $Py=\eta(\eta^Ty)/\|\eta\|^2$ belongs to $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$, and $\eta^T(y-Py)=0$, so $y-Py\in(\operatorname{span}\{\eta\})^\perp$. Thus $P$ is the rank-one orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ in [F4]. The conclusion concerns only the joint law of $T,Z$, so by [F1] it suffices to use the realization $Y=\mu+\sigma W$ with $W\sim N_n(0,I_n)$. Apply [F2] to $P$. This use of AC is exactly [A1].

Because $P\eta=\eta$, $T=\eta^T\mu+\sigma\eta^TPW$, while $Z=(I_n-P)\mu+\sigma(I_n-P)W$. Thus $T$ and $Z$ are measurable functions of the independent vectors $PW$ and $(I_n-P)W$; [F3] makes them independent.

By the linear-projection clause of [F1], $T=\eta^TY$ is normal with mean $\eta^T\mu$ and variance $\eta^T(\sigma^2I_n)\eta=\sigma^2\|\eta\|^2$. AC is inherited from [A1] through the normal-law supplier [F1].

boundaries.reason: The Statement fixes n>=1 and eta nonzero; no empty-dimensional Gaussian vector is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: For n=1 the residual is the constant zero vector; step 2.1 proves independence through measurable functions of the independent projection components.
When n=1, step 3.1 gives the nondegenerate scalar contrast law and step 2.1 allows a zero residual.
The residual may be degenerate when n=1; step 2.1 includes the constant residual case, while sigma>0 and eta nonzero keep T nondegenerate.

boundaries.reason: No interval or limiting endpoint appears in the theorem.

boundaries.evidence: AC is explicit and is used through the multivariate normal representation and orthogonal-projection supplier in steps 1.1 and 3.1.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts independence and a marginal law, not an equivalence.
The theorem asserts independence and a marginal law, not an equivalence.

axiom_uses.reason: AC is inherited through the multivariate-normal representation and the Gaussian orthogonal-projection supplier; the measurable-function independence step adds no stronger principle.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all three proof steps and current projection, multivariate-normal and measurable-independence suppliers. P is self-adjoint idempotent rank one; law-realization transfer is legitimate and T,Z are affine Borel images of independent projected Gaussian blocks. Scalar variance is sigma squared times norm eta squared, strictly positive. n=1 gives constant residual and is covered by rank n supplier case. AC inherited from Gaussian construction/projection. No reader/refuter finding or defect.

$$Ay\le b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G(Z(y))\ \text{and}\ L(Z(y))\le T(y)\le U(Z(y)).$$
The functions $L,U$ are Borel measurable as extended-real-valued functions, and the set of pairs $(t,z)$ satisfying the right-hand side is Borel.

Assume AC. Let $Y\sim N_n(\mu,\sigma^2I_n)$ with known $\sigma>0$, and fix $\eta\ne0$. With $T=\eta^TY$, $P_\eta=\eta\eta^T/\|\eta\|^2$, and $Z=(I_n-P_\eta)Y$ as in [[def-polyhedral-selection-event-and-contrast-interval]], the scalar $T$ and vector $Z$ are independent, and
$$T\sim N(\eta^T\mu,\sigma^2\|\eta\|^2).$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

Assume AC. In the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selection-event-and-contrast-interval]], let $Y\sim N_n(\mu,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $\sigma>0$ is known ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]). Put $\theta=\eta^T\mu$, $s=\sigma\|\eta\|$, and let $\Phi$ be the standard normal CDF from [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]. Extend it by $\Phi(-\infty)=0$ and $\Phi(+\infty)=1$. For a candidate contrast value $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\Delta_\vartheta(z)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{U(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{L(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right).$$
When $G(z)$ holds, $L(z)<U(z)$, and $\Delta_\vartheta(z)>0$, define
$$q_\vartheta(t,z)=\frac{\Phi((t-\vartheta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\vartheta)/s)}{\Delta_\vartheta(z)}\qquad (L(z)\le t\le U(z)).$$
For a total statistic on $\mathbb R^n$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=0$ when $y\notin S$ or when the denominator is zero; on the remaining part of $S$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=q_\vartheta(T(y),Z(y))$. The value assigned on zero-normalizer fibers is only a measurable extension; when $P_\mu(S)>0$, the conditional law given selection gives those fibers probability zero.

Under $P_\mu$, $T$ and $Z$ are independent by [F2], so their joint law is the product of their marginal laws by [F3]. Write $
u_T=N(	heta,s^2)$ and let $
u_Z$ be the marginal law of $Z$. Both are probability measures and hence sigma-finite. By [F1] and [F7], the selection event in these coordinates is the Borel set $D=\{(t,z):G(z),\ L(z)\le t\le U(z)\}$. For every product-measurable set $B$, conditioning the product law on $D$ gives $Q_\mu((T,Z)\in B)=\int_B\mathbf 1_D(t,z)/P_\mu(S)\,d(
u_T	imes
u_Z)(t,z)$. Thus the selected joint law has this product density.

Put $H(z)=G(z)\land(L(z)\le U(z))$. If $H(z)$ fails, the fiber is empty and its section integral is zero. If $H(z)$ holds, the section is $[L(z),U(z)]$; by [F5], [F6], and the endpoint convention in [F7], its $
u_T$-probability is $\Delta_	heta(z)$, including a singleton interval and infinite endpoints. Thus the section integral of the selected density is $m(z)=\mathbf 1_{H(z)}\Delta_	heta(z)/P_\mu(S)$. It is finite because $0\le\Delta_	heta(z)\le1$ on feasible fibers and $P_\mu(S)>0$. Apply [F4] with filler probability $
u_T$: for almost every selected $z$, $m(z)>0$, so $H(z)$ holds, $L(z)<U(z)$, and $\Delta_	heta(z)>0$; the conditional law of $T$ is $K_z(B)=
u_T(B\cap[L(z),U(z)])/\Delta_	heta(z)$. Fibers with zero section integral have zero selected marginal probability, so their arbitrary extension value in the pivot definition is immaterial.

For $L(z)\le t\le U(z)$, [F6] gives $K_z((-\infty,t])=[\Phi((t-\theta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\theta)/s)]/[\Phi((U(z)-\theta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\theta)/s)]=q_\theta(t,z)$. The denominator is positive exactly on the selected fibers under consideration. The finite max/min formulas make $L,U,G$ Borel, and [F5] with [F7] makes $\Delta_\theta$ Borel. On the Borel set of $y\in S$ for which $G(Z(y))$, $L(Z(y))<U(Z(y))$, and $\Delta_\theta(Z(y))>0$, the pivot's numerator and reciprocal denominator are Borel, so the ratio is Borel; the definition extends it by zero on the complement.

Fix such a $z$. The conditional density in step 2.1 is positive throughout the interval and has no atoms; [F5] makes its CDF continuous and strictly increasing from zero to one, including when an endpoint is infinite. For any $u\in(0,1)$ there is a unique $t_u$ in the interval with $q_\theta(t_u,z)=u$, so $K_z\{t:q_\theta(t,z)\le u\}=K_z((-\infty,t_u])=q_\theta(t_u,z)=u$. At $u=0$ the probability is zero and at $u=1$ it is one because the conditional law has a density. Thus the pivot is uniform given $Z=z,S$.

Integrating the conditional identity in step 4.1 against the selected marginal law of $Z$ supplied by [F4] gives $P_\mu(q_\theta(Y)\le u\mid S)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. Hence the pivot is uniform given $S$ as well.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], with $P_\mu(S)>0$. For $P_\mu(Z\in\cdot\mid S)$-almost every $z$, the conditional law of $T$ given $Z=z$ and $S$ is the $N(\theta,s^2)$ law restricted to $[L(z),U(z)]$ and normalized by $\Delta_\theta(z)>0$. Its CDF on that interval is $q_\theta(t,z)$. The pivot is Borel measurable on the selected data space. Consequently $q_\theta(Y)$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $(Z,S)$ wherever the normalizer is positive, and is also Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $S$ alone. The event $S$ is a single fixed polyhedron; no union-of-polyhedra claim is made.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal Y,\mathcal G),\mathcal M,(Q_\mu)_{\mu\in\mathcal M})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let $\tau:\mathcal M\to\Lambda$ be a parameter functional. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, a set-valued procedure $C:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal P(\Lambda)$ is a selective confidence set with coverage at least $1-\alpha$ if, for every $\mu\in\mathcal M$, its membership section $\{y:\tau(\mu)\in C(y)\}$ belongs to $\mathcal G$ and
$$Q_\mu\{y:\tau(\mu)\in C(y)\}\ge1-\alpha.$$
It is exact if equality holds for every $\mu$. Here the laws $Q_\mu$ are the laws after conditioning on the specified selection event. When $\mathcal M\ne\varnothing$, the pullback $D(y)=\{\mu\in\mathcal M:\tau(\mu)\in C(y)\}$ is a confidence-set procedure as in [[def-confidence-set-and-coverage]], with the same membership sections and coverage at each $\mu$. When $\mathcal M=\varnothing$, the stated coverage and exactness requirements are vacuous. No measurable structure on $\mathcal M$ or $\Lambda$ is imposed.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a parameter-indexed family of measurable
real-valued quantities with a common sampling law. The maps $q_\theta$
may depend on the unknown parameter. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

derivations.claim: For any $\mu$ in the conditional experiment, [F1] gives $q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ under $Q_\mu$. For $0\le u\le1$, the event $2\min\{q,1-q\}\le u$ is the union of the two tails $q\le u/2$ and $q\ge1-u/2$, whose uniform probabilities sum to $u$ (their intersection has measure zero). Thus, if $H_0(\vartheta)\ne\varnothing$, $p_\vartheta$ is uniform under every null law and is measurable by the pivot formula; [F2] makes it a valid p-value.

If $H_0(\vartheta)\ne\varnothing$ and the alternative is nonempty, [F3] applied to $p_\vartheta$ gives conditional size at most $\alpha$. By [F4] size is the supremum of the null rejection probabilities; since every null law has the exact uniform p-value distribution from step 1.1, $Q_\mu(p_\vartheta\le\alpha)=\alpha$ for every null $\mu$, so the size is exactly $\alpha$.

By [F1], [F6], and [F8], $q_\mu(Y):=q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)$ is a pivot in the conditional experiment. Its full-parameter inversion is $C_{\rm full}(Y)=\{\mu'\in\Theta_S:q_{\eta^T\mu'}(Y)\in[\alpha/2,1-\alpha/2]\}$. The acceptance interval has uniform probability $1-\alpha$, so [F7] gives exact coverage for $C_{\rm full}$. Its image under $\mu'\mapsto\eta^T\mu'$ is exactly $C_\eta(Y)$ by the definition of $\Theta_\eta$. For each fixed true $\mu$, membership $\eta^T\mu\in C_\eta(Y)$ is precisely $\alpha/2\le q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)\le1-\alpha/2$, which has $Q_\mu$-probability $1-\alpha$ by [F1]. The membership section is measurable by the Borel pivot formula, so [F5] applies.

boundaries.evidence: The p-value and conditional type-I-error claims require a nonempty point null; the size conclusion explicitly requires both that null and the alternative to be nonempty, matching the hypotheses of the size definition and the p-value test theorem.
At alpha=0, the Uniform pivot gives zero rejection probability and the central acceptance interval is all of [0,1]; steps 1.1 and 3.1 cover these endpoints.
At alpha=1, the threshold test rejects with probability one and the central acceptance interval has uniform probability zero; steps 2.1 and 3.1 include alpha=1.
The Statement has s=sigma||eta||>0, and step 1.1 uses the positive selection event and conditional-uniform theorem; the contrast pivot is not degenerate.
The full range alpha in [0,1] is included in steps 1.1-3.1, with the two-sided tails meeting only at a null point when alpha=1.
AC is inherited through the Gaussian pivot theorem and appears in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1; no additional witness selection is used.

No equivalence is asserted; the proof establishes test validity and exact coverage.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge0$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and a fixed nonzero vector $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise. Define the projection matrix and contrast direction
$$P_\eta=\frac{\eta\eta^T}{\|\eta\|^2},\qquad c_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\|\eta\|^2}.$$
The matrix $P_\eta$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, put
$$T(y)=\eta^Ty,\qquad Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y.$$
Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

For row $j$ of $A$, written $a_j^T$, define
$$r_j=a_j^Tc_\eta,\qquad d_j(z)=b_j-a_j^Tz.$$
Let $J_-=\{j:r_j<0\}$, $J_+=\{j:r_j>0\}$, and $J_0=\{j:r_j=0\}$. Define
$$L(z)=\begin{cases}\max_{j\in J_-}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_-\ne\varnothing,\\-\infty,&J_-=\varnothing,\end{cases}\qquad U(z)=\begin{cases}\min_{j\in J_+}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_+\ne\varnothing,\\+\infty,&J_+=\varnothing.\end{cases}$$
Define $G(z)$ to hold exactly when $d_j(z)\ge0$ for every $j\in J_0$. The selection event is $S=\{y:Ay\le b\}$. The interval associated with $z$ is $I(z)=\varnothing$ if $G(z)$ fails or $L(z)>U(z)$, and is $[L(z),U(z)]$ otherwise. The next lemma proves that this interval describes precisely the fiber of $S$ along the contrast direction.

Assume AC. In the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selection-event-and-contrast-interval]], let $Y\sim N_n(\mu,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $\sigma>0$ is known ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]). Put $\theta=\eta^T\mu$, $s=\sigma\|\eta\|$, and let $\Phi$ be the standard normal CDF from [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]. Extend it by $\Phi(-\infty)=0$ and $\Phi(+\infty)=1$. For a candidate contrast value $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\Delta_\vartheta(z)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{U(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{L(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right).$$
When $G(z)$ holds, $L(z)<U(z)$, and $\Delta_\vartheta(z)>0$, define
$$q_\vartheta(t,z)=\frac{\Phi((t-\vartheta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\vartheta)/s)}{\Delta_\vartheta(z)}\qquad (L(z)\le t\le U(z)).$$
For a total statistic on $\mathbb R^n$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=0$ when $y\notin S$ or when the denominator is zero; on the remaining part of $S$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=q_\vartheta(T(y),Z(y))$. The value assigned on zero-normalizer fibers is only a measurable extension; when $P_\mu(S)>0$, the conditional law given selection gives those fibers probability zero.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], with $P_\mu(S)>0$. For $P_\mu(Z\in\cdot\mid S)$-almost every $z$, the conditional law of $T$ given $Z=z$ and $S$ is the $N(\theta,s^2)$ law restricted to $[L(z),U(z)]$ and normalized by $\Delta_\theta(z)>0$. Its CDF on that interval is $q_\theta(t,z)$. The pivot is Borel measurable on the selected data space. Consequently $q_\theta(Y)$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $(Z,S)$ wherever the normalizer is positive, and is also Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $S$ alone. The event $S$ is a single fixed polyhedron; no union-of-polyhedra claim is made.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], and suppose $P_\mu(S)>0$ for at least one $\mu\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\Theta_S=\{\mu\in\mathbb R^n:P_\mu(S)>0\}$. The selected sample space is $S$ with trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(S)=\{S\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\}$, and for $\mu\in\Theta_S$ let $Q_\mu=P_\mu(\,\cdot\mid S)$ be the conditional sampling law. For $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$p_\vartheta(Y)=2\min\{q_\vartheta(Y),1-q_\vartheta(Y)\}.$$
For the point null $H_0(\vartheta)=\{\mu\in\Theta_S:\eta^T\mu=\vartheta\}$, assume $H_0(\vartheta)\ne\varnothing$. Then $p_\vartheta$ is a valid p-value in the conditional experiment $(Q_\mu)$ and is Uniform$(0,1)$ under every null law. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, rejecting when $p_\vartheta\le\alpha$ has conditional type-I error exactly $\alpha$. If, in addition, a nonempty alternative $\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta_S\setminus H_0(\vartheta)$ is specified, the test has size $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$.

For $0\le\alpha\le1$, put $\Theta_\eta=\{\eta^T\mu:\mu\in\Theta_S\}$ and
$$C_\eta(Y)=\{\vartheta\in\Theta_\eta:\alpha/2\le q_\vartheta(Y)\le1-\alpha/2\}.$$
This is an exact selective confidence set for the functional $\tau(\mu)=\eta^T\mu$ in the sense of [[def-exact-selective-confidence-set-for-a-functional]]: for every $\mu$ with $P_\mu(S)>0$,
$$Q_\mu\{\eta^T\mu\in C_\eta(Y)\}=1-\alpha.$$
The guarantee is for one fixed contrast and one fixed selection event, not simultaneous coverage over a selected family.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The model is the isotropic Gaussian construction in [F8]; [F5] gives each scalar marginal as an affine image of a standard normal. For $\sigma>0$, [F6] gives $P_\mu(1<Y_1\le2)=\Phi((2-\mu_1)/\sigma)-\Phi((1-\mu_1)/\sigma)>0$ and $P_\mu(0<Y_2\le1)=\Phi((1-\mu_2)/\sigma)-\Phi((0-\mu_2)/\sigma)>0$. By [F7], the rectangle $(1,2]\times(0,1]$ has probability equal to the product of these positive probabilities; it lies in $S$, so $P_\mu(S)>0$. Here $c_\eta=(1,0)^T$. The single row has $r_1=(-1,1)c_\eta=-1$ and, at $z=(0,Y_2)$, $d_1(z)=-Y_2$. Thus $L(z)=d_1(z)/r_1=Y_2$, there are no upper constraints so $U(z)=+\infty$, and $G(z)$ is true. The event is exactly $Y_1\ge Y_2$, giving interval $[Y_2,+\infty)$.

Since $T=Y_1$, $\theta=\mu_1$, and $s=\sigma$, the definition [F2] gives $q_{\vartheta}(Y_1,Y_2)=[\Phi((Y_1-\vartheta)/\sigma)-\Phi((Y_2-\vartheta)/\sigma)]/[1-\Phi((Y_2-\vartheta)/\sigma)]$. At $(Y_1,Y_2)=(1,0)$, $\sigma=1$, and $\vartheta=0$, this becomes the displayed $q_0$.

Under the point null $\mu_1=0$, [F3] makes $q_0$ Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on selection, so [F4] gives the stated two-sided p-value and exact selective test. For general $\vartheta$, the set retaining $\alpha/2\le q_\vartheta\le1-\alpha/2$ has conditional coverage $1-\alpha$ by [F4]. No claim about a selected-family simultaneous guarantee is used.
